title: Before you go
hookLine: anyone is welcome; cover your head, take off your shoes, bring no tobacco or alcohol

lines: WHAT IF I GET IT WRONG?
cards: Where do I stand? What do I touch? What if I do something wrong and everybody notices?

Those are the questions of anyone stepping into a stranger's kitchen, or a stranger's place of prayer. Someone curious can drive past a gurdwara for years and never go in, because nobody told them the rules.
So before the next week of visiting, here's what to know before you go. And the first thing comes first for a reason. You're allowed in.

teach.b: Gurdwara means the door of the Guru, the Guru's gateway. It's the Sikh place of worship, and its doors are open to everyone: Sikhs, people of any other faith, people of none. That openness is written into Sikh history.
The Harmandir Sahib in Amritsar, the Golden Temple, was built with entrances on all four sides, and Sikhs read that as a welcome to people from every direction and every background.

It's also set lower than the ground around it, so you step down to enter, which tradition reads as humility. So what do you actually do? A few things, all about respect for the Guru Granth Sahib, present in the main hall.
Cover your head: men, women and children all do. A scarf, a bandana, anything that covers the hair; gurdwaras often keep a basket of head coverings by the door. Take off your shoes.
There's usually a shoe rack or a room for them, often a place to wash your hands, and sometimes your feet.

Bring no tobacco, alcohol or drugs, not even in a pocket: the Sikh code of conduct forbids tobacco and intoxicants, and they don't come into the gurdwara. Dress modestly, and expect to sit on the floor. That's it.

Nobody will ask what you believe, or ask you to join anything. If you're unsure what to do next, ask, and someone will usually show you, often with a plate of food to follow. Hospitality is part of what a gurdwara is for.

how: Visitors of any faith are welcome in a gurdwara; they cover their heads, remove their shoes, wash their hands, bring no tobacco or alcohol, and sit on the floor in the main hall.

practice: If you have a map app, search for gurdwara and see how far the closest one is; there are gurdwaras far beyond Punjab, in small towns as well as big cities.
Or just picture arriving at one: slipping off your shoes, tying a scarf over your hair, washing your hands, stepping inside. Notice what you feel: curiosity, nerves, or both.
